newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Croatia criticised for shunning Balkan group.
newsitem.headline: Croatia criticised for shunning Balkan group.

text.p: Croatia's refusal to join a U.S. initiative on regional economic integration in southeast Europe is a mistake, the president of the U.S.-Yugoslavia Economic Council said on Friday.
"Croatia is the last holdout. It is a big mistake for them. They cannot wish themselves out of their geographical position," John Scanlon, a former U.S. ambassador to former Yugoslavia, told Reuters.
"Being a member of the Southeast European Cooperative Initiative (SECI) does not mean Croatia will be reintegrated politically into the Balkans, if that's the issue it is concerned about," he said.

Croatia, which seceded from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia in 1991, has insisted it is a central European, not a Balkan country, and believes SECI would drag it back into a Yugoslav framework undermining its hard-won sovereignty.

SECI was launched by the United States late last year to promote regional economic cooperation, helping re-establish a durable peace in the Balkans after four years of nationalist wars within former Yugoslavia.
Scanlon, attending a business gathering in Belgrade, said SECI was a commendable project because it would lower or remove trade barriers and deal with problems in a cooperative way.
"This would be an advantage to Croatia too. But at the moment it is mired to some extent to its political obstinacy."
Macedonia, Slovenia and Bosnia, three of four ex-Yugoslav republics which seceded in 1991-92, have endorsed SECI.
The remaining Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, is not a SECI member yet.
"Yugoslavia is an observer and could become a member once political problems are resolved," Scanlon said.
A U.S.-imposed "outer wall" of sanctions, still in place after a war-related U.N. embargo against Belgrade was lifted in 1996, bars the country's return to international organisations.

The main prerequisites for Belgrade's full reintegration into the world community include cooperation with the U.N. war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia, improved human rights in Serbia's Albanian-majority province of Kosovo, and progress in talks on a shareout of former Yugoslav assets.
"I would like to see all barriers to trade and economic development in southeast Europe disappear," Scanlon said.
